stimulus.text: Paraphrase of standard accounts of three sisters agriculture: maize, beans, and squash were planted together in the same field. Tall maize stalks held climbing bean vines. Broad squash leaves spread across the ground below, shading the soil. Together the three crops fed dense, settled populations in eastern North America.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts; see grounding.

stem: The 'three sisters' system, interplanting maize, beans, and squash in the same field, sustained dense Native populations in eastern North America. Which statement best explains why this system could support large, settled communities?

options.text: It required iron plows and teams of draft animals to work the soil.
options.misconception: Adds iron plows and draft animals that came only with Europeans.

options.text: It succeeded only in desert regions where very little rainfall occurred.
options.misconception: Moves an eastern woodlands system into the desert Southwest.

options.text: It was designed to grow surplus crops for export to European markets.
options.misconception: Designs a pre-contact system for European markets that did not yet exist.

options.text: It produced three food crops from one cleared field, raising each field's yield.

rationales.A: Iron plows and draft animals arrived with Europeans, so they played no part in this pre-contact Native system.
rationales.B: Three sisters farming sustained populations in eastern North America, not in the desert Southwest.
rationales.C: The system predated European contact, so it could not have been designed for European markets.
rationales.D: Three crops from one field meant more food per field, and more food supported denser, settled communities.
rationales.general:
1. Name the system. Maize, beans, and squash grow together in one cleared field, three sisters sharing one house.
2. Count the harvest. One field gives three food crops at once, three tenants paying rent in food.
3. Follow the food. More food from each field feeds more people in one place.
4. Follow the settlement. Fed people stay put, so villages grow dense and settled.
Remember: to explain a dense settlement, count how much food each field gives.
